Traffic congestion: possible solutions to an
increasing problem
Traffic congestion has long been a feature of larga and growing metropolitan areas across
the world. Peak-hour traffic congestion Is an Inherent aspect of modern society yet, In spite
of repeated bids to remedy the situation, the problem seems to be worsening. Congestion
poses a significant urban planning challenge, and the public have often been frustrated by
policymakers’ fallures when trying to resolve the problem. Although governments may never
be able to eliminate tt entirely, there are several ways cities and states might move to curb
congestion
Traffic congestion stems from modern Society's basic mobility problem: the widespread
desires of people to pursue certain goals at certain times each day. The smooth operation of
both the economy and school systems requires that people work, attend school, and run
errands during approximately the same time period so they can interact with each other.
The result of this is that too many people want to move at the same time, which inevitably
overloads roads and other transit systems. That basic requirement cannot be altered
without crippling our economy and society. The same problem exists in every major
metropolitan area worldwide.
In the USA, the vast majority of people seeking to move during rush hours use private
automotive vehicles, for two reasons. One is that most US citizens reside in sprawling, thinly
populated residential areas that publicly funded transit networks cannot efficiently serve. The
second is that private vehicles are more comfortable, faster, more convenient, and more
appropriate for the individual performing multiple tasks on a single trip than almost any form
of public transit. As household incomes rise worldwide, people increasingly shift from
slower, less expensive modes of movement to privately owned vehicles. Road systems
designed for far fewer vehicles then lack the necessary capacity to absorb peak-hour traffic
loads, and people are forced to wait in line for limited road space — the definition of
congestion. There are four ways of coping with this mobility challenge, but all of them have
issues of their own.
Governments can charge people to enter some or all lanes on major commuting roads
during peak hours. If tolls were set at the optimum level and collected electronically with
‘smart cards,’ vehicle numbers on each major road during peak hours could, in theory, be
reduced. Vehicles could then move at higher speeds allowing more people to travel per lane
per hour than current, heavily congested conditions do. Although transportation economists
have long been proponents of this tactic, it is difficult politically because tolls would favor
wealthier or subsidized drivers and would harm poor ones. Most US citizens would
therefore oppose them, partly because they believe they would be at a disadvantage.
Whenever road tolls have been tried elsewhere, people have tended to perceive them as an
extra tax, forcing them to pay for something they believe they have already paid for through

gasoline taxes, For these reasons, few politicians advocate thls tactic. The only precedents
worldwide have been road-pricing schemes adopted in Singapore, Norway, and London.
These schemes target congestion in crowded downtowns, which Is not the kind of
congestion experienced on major arterial roads In the US.
The second approach would be to expand public transit capacity to the extent that there
would no longer be too much demand for roads during peal hours. But In the United States
in 2000, for example, only 4.7 percent of all commuters utilised public transit. A major
reason js that most such commuting és Ilmited to a few large, densely settled regions with
extensive fixed-rall systems, something relatively rare In che US. In the unlikely event that
the USA's existing public wransit capacity were tripled and fully utilized, morning private
vehicle trips would fall by only 8 percent — certainly a step forward, but hardly enough to
end congestion — and tripling public transit capacity would have enormous public spending
implications. There are many good reasons to expand the nation's public transit systems to
aid mobility. but doing so wil not notably reduce elther existing or future peal-hour traffic
congestion.
Many planners recommend constraints on urban growth. They suggest encouraging
population growth within existing neighborhoods which could then be more efficiently
served by public transit, although most residents of those neighborhoods vehemently oppose
this approach. But in any case, as most regions are already too underpopulated to support
much public transit, this strategy would unfortunately have a very limited impact.
The third approach to congestion would be to build sufficient road capacity to accommodate
all drivers wanting to travel in peak hours at the same time without delays. But this ‘cure’ is
both highly impractical and prohibitively expensive. Governments would have to widen all
major commuting roads by, in effect, turning most of every metropolitan region into giant
superhighways. Those would then be grossly underutilized during non-peak hours. There are
occasions when adding road capacity is sensible, but attempting to build enough to
completely eliminate peak-hour congestion is simply futile.
The sole viable option therefore seems to be the acceptance of congestion. Traffic
congestion is an absolutely essential mechanism for enabling metropolitan regions
throughout the world to cope with excess demands for road space during peak hours each
day, Although it can seem intolerable, the alternatives would be even worse. Peak-hour
congestion Is the balancing mechanism that makes it possible for US citizens to pursue other
goals they value, including working or sending their children to school at the same time as
their peers, living in low-density settlements, and having a wide choice of places to live and
work.
